svg.text: Backend – how concurrent requests are divided, and where state is kept
These two choices decide performance characteristics and vulnerability classes together
Concurrency models
Processes (prefork)
A separate memory space per request.
+ one dying leaves the rest alive · strong isolation
- memory cost · low concurrency ceiling
The trap: keep state in process memory and each
request may land on a different process.
Thread pool
Sharing memory makes it light.
+ more concurrent requests than processes
- shared state = a stage for race conditions
Place a global cache, counter or user context
wrongly and data mixes between requests.
Event loop (single-threaded async)

g.text: waiting I/O is handed off, not held

svg.text: Most web requests are waiting, not computing.
+ memory barely grows with connection count
- one long CPU-bound piece stops everything
Mix in a synchronous library and the advantage
vanishes entirely – the most common mistake.
Where the login state is kept
Sessions – the server remembers
The cookie holds only an identifier; the real data sits in the server store.
+ immediate invalidation – delete it from the store and it is done
+ the contents are not exposed to the client
- the server holds state → horizontal scaling needs a shared store
Against fixation and theft: reissue the session ID at login, enough entropy,
discard server-side on logout (deleting the client cookie is not enough)
Tokens (JWT) – the token itself carries the content
Signed JSON. The server verifies the signature and judges without a lookup.
+ stateless – many servers can verify with no store
- an issued token cannot be revoked → offset with short expiry + refresh tokens
- the content is signed, not hidden – anyone can read it
Recurring verification failures: accepting alg=none · RS256→HS256 confusion ·
trusting kid/jku to fetch the key externally · not checking expiry
OAuth 2.0 and OIDC – the two most often mixed up
OAuth 2.0 = authorization
The delegation "this app may access my resources". It does not say who the user is.
OIDC = authentication
Puts an ID token on OAuth to standardize "who this user is".
What OAuth 2.1 (still an IETF draft as of 2026) makes mandatory – every item back-calculated from a real incident
PKCE required · exact redirect URI match · refresh token rotation required · implicit and password grants removed · no bearer tokens in query strings
The substance of the revision is "promoting optional security recommendations to required". A decision made on the premise that deployed implementations do not follow recommendations.
